title: Learning algorithms that extrapolate beyond training lengths
open: Can we characterize the training distributions and inductive biases that yield learning algorithms whose performance persists on inputs substantially longer than any seen during training? More precisely, when do the performance curves — and ideally formal guarantees — extend beyond the lengths used for training and model selection?
status: Systematic-generalization failures have been studied since at least 2017 (Lake and Baroni, 2017/2018, *Generalization without systematicity*, arXiv:1711.00350), and scratchpads offer a useful partial mechanism (Nye et al., 2021, *Show Your Work*, arXiv:2112.00114). However, success on selected arithmetic tasks does not establish general length extrapolation.
solved_when: There is an identified pairing of a training distribution and inductive bias for which performance curves, and where possible guarantees, hold at input lengths substantially exceeding those used for training and model selection.
why: A solution would support reliable reasoning over larger programs, documents, graphs, and proofs.
key_works: Lake and Baroni, 2017/2018, *Generalization without systematicity*, arXiv:1711.00350; Nye et al., 2021, *Show Your Work*, arXiv:2112.00114.

bib.title: Learning algorithms that extrapolate beyond training lengths

title: Predicting grokking before generalization occurs
open: Can we predict, before it happens, whether a memorizing network will grok — that is, forecast the transition time to generalization and distinguish eventual generalization from permanent overfitting, using only measurements available prior to the transition? The predictor should be task-, optimizer-, architecture-, and scale-transferable.
status: Grokking was documented by Power et al. (2022, *Grokking: Generalization Beyond Overfitting on Small Algorithmic Datasets*, arXiv:2201.02177) on small algorithmic datasets. Current explanations address individual examples, which is weaker than forecasting transition times and distinguishing eventual generalization from permanent overfitting.
solved_when: A method exists that, from pre-transition measurements, forecasts the transition time and correctly decides whether generalization will occur at all, and this predictor transfers across tasks, optimizers, architectures, and training scales.
why: It would avoid wasted training compute and expose which internal structures in a network support abstraction.
key_works: Power et al., 2022, *Grokking: Generalization Beyond Overfitting on Small Algorithmic Datasets*, arXiv:2201.02177.

bib.title: Predicting grokking before generalization occurs

title: Deployment-relevant generalization certificates
open: Can we compute a generalization bound for a practically trained LLM that actually predicts how the model will behave in deployment, including under realistic distribution shifts? Such a certificate should rank models informatively — separating better from worse models — rather than merely landing below a trivial ceiling.
status: Non-vacuous bounds already exist: 2023 work (Lotfi et al., *Non-Vacuous Generalization Bounds for Large Language Models*, arXiv:2312.17173) addressed large compressed models, and 2024 token-level bounds (Lotfi et al., *Unlocking Tokens as Data Points for Generalization Bounds on Larger Language Models*, arXiv:2407.18158) reached compressed LLaMA2-70B. The remaining target is tightness and deployment relevance, not the existence of any non-vacuous bound; a related statistical challenge is informative risk bounds under dependent sampling.
solved_when: A computable, non-vacuous generalization bound exists for practically trained (not just compressed) LLMs that both accounts for important distribution shifts and meaningfully predicts downstream error, distinguishing better from worse models instead of only beating a trivial ceiling.
why: It would give a mathematical complement to benchmark-based assurance, replacing purely empirical evaluation with provable deployment-relevant guarantees.
key_works: Lotfi et al., 2023, *Non-Vacuous Generalization Bounds for Large Language Models*, arXiv:2312.17173; Lotfi et al., 2024, *Unlocking Tokens as Data Points for Generalization Bounds on Larger Language Models*, arXiv:2407.18158.

bib.title: Deployment-relevant generalization certificates

title: Distinguishing genuine capability transitions from measurement artifacts
open: How can we tell whether a language model has genuinely undergone a qualitative change in its learned computation, rather than the apparent transition being an artifact of how we measure it? Develop tests that distinguish real transitions from effects of thresholding, discontinuous scoring, data contamination, or sparse sampling of model sizes, and specify in advance what observations would falsify an emergence claim.
status: The 2023 "mirage" analysis (Schaeffer, Miranda, and Koyejo, 2023, *Are Emergent Abilities of Large Language Models a Mirage?*, arXiv:2304.15004) demonstrated that some apparent emergence depends on the choice of metric; it does not establish that every qualitative transition is an artifact.
solved_when: A validated test procedure exists that can discriminate genuine qualitative transitions from the named artifact sources (thresholding, discontinuous scoring, contamination, sparse model-size sampling), together with explicit falsification criteria for emergence claims.
why: It sharpens scaling forecasts and prevents capability narratives from being driven by artifacts of the measuring instrument rather than the model.
key_works: Schaeffer, Miranda, and Koyejo, 2023, *Are Emergent Abilities of Large Language Models a Mirage?*, arXiv:2304.15004; Kaplan et al., 2020, *Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models*, arXiv:2001.08361.

bib.title: Distinguishing genuine capability transitions from measurement artifacts

title: Scaling-law transfer across domains
subfield: Scaling laws, optimization, and resource allocation
open: Can we predict a model's downstream capability from small experiments when the target domain, data mixture, or evaluation distribution differs substantially from the regime where the scaling law was fitted? In formal terms, this asks for a transfer method whose predictions carry calibrated extrapolation uncertainty rather than point estimates that hold only under interpolation within a training family.
status: Power-law descriptions of neural language model scaling date to 2020 (Kaplan et al., 2020, arXiv:2001.08361), and subsequent work has tested scaling under overtraining and on downstream tasks (Gadre et al., 2024, arXiv:2403.08540). However, existing results largely interpolate within a training family; reliable transfer to new domains and architectures remains a strictly stronger, unmet requirement.
solved_when: A method exists that predicts downstream capability on substantially different domains, data mixtures, or evaluation distributions from small experiments, with quantified, calibrated extrapolation uncertainty on those predictions.
why: It would let practitioners kill doomed configurations cheaply and allocate compute confidently, reducing the number of expensive failed training programs.
key_works: Kaplan et al., 2020, *Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models*, arXiv:2001.08361; Gadre et al., 2024, *Language models scale reliably with over-training and on downstream tasks*, arXiv:2403.08540.

bib.title: Scaling-law transfer across domains

title: Hyperparameter transfer across architectural changes
subfield: Scaling laws, optimization, and resource allocation
open: When a model's width, depth, sequence length, numerical precision, and architecture all change at once, can a known set of hyperparameters — learning rates, initialization, regularization, and optimizer settings — be transferred predictably? The goal is a rule that quantifies exactly where such transfer fails and provides inexpensive corrective measurements to repair it.
status: μP demonstrated valuable zero-shot transfer across model widths in 2022 (Yang et al., 2022, *Tensor Programs V: Tuning Large Neural Networks via Zero-Shot Hyperparameter Transfer*, arXiv:2203.03466). A general transfer rule covering all of these changes remains open and is a substantially stronger target.
solved_when: A general transfer rule exists that covers simultaneous changes in width, depth, sequence length, precision, and architecture, specifies quantitatively where transfer fails, and comes with cheap corrective measurements, going beyond width-only transfer.
why: It cuts the cost and instability of scaling experiments, since hyperparameters would no longer need to be retuned from scratch after each architectural change.
key_works: Yang et al., 2022, *Tensor Programs V: Tuning Large Neural Networks via Zero-Shot Hyperparameter Transfer*, arXiv:2203.03466.

bib.title: Hyperparameter transfer across architectural changes

title: Tenfold reduction in unique training-data requirements
subfield: Scaling laws, optimization, and resource allocation
open: Can a model trained on one-tenth as much unique data match a preregistered baseline's broad, contamination-controlled performance — with the information budget honestly accounted for, so no equivalent information is smuggled in through teachers or synthetic-data generators?
status: Data-mixture optimization (e.g., Xie et al., 2023, *DoReMi*, arXiv:2305.10429) and large-scale curation (e.g., Penedo et al., 2024, *The FineWeb Datasets*, arXiv:2406.17557) deliver measurable improvements, but a broad tenfold information-efficiency gain under explicit information accounting remains an open moonshot.
solved_when: A model trained on at most one-tenth the baseline's unique training data matches that preregistered baseline on a broad, contamination-controlled evaluation suite, under an explicit accounting showing teachers and synthetic-data generators contributed no equivalent hidden information.
why: A tenfold gain in data efficiency would make capable models feasible for domains and languages where large unique corpora simply do not exist.
key_works: Xie et al., 2023, *DoReMi*, arXiv:2305.10429; Penedo et al., 2024, *The FineWeb Datasets*, arXiv:2406.17557.

bib.title: Tenfold reduction in unique training-data requirements

title: Preserving rare tails during synthetic augmentation
subfield: Training data, provenance, and synthetic-data dynamics
open: Can training on repeatedly recycled synthetic data preserve the rare tails of the distribution — uncommon facts, dialects, failure cases, and decision boundaries — rather than just its bulk? A rigorous demonstration must show tail preservation as distinct from, and not implied by, average benchmark performance.
status: Recursive-training studies (Shumailov et al., 2023, *The Curse of Recursion*, arXiv:2305.17493) identify distributional degradation, while data accumulation (Gerstgrasser et al., 2024, *Is Model Collapse Inevitable?*, arXiv:2404.01413) mitigates some collapse regimes. Tail-specific guarantees and realistic rare-event evaluations remain distinct, unmet targets.
solved_when: A synthetic-augmentation regime is exhibited in which rare but important content (facts, dialects, failure cases, decision boundaries) measurably survives across repeated augmentation cycles, with tail-specific evaluations reported separately from aggregate benchmark scores.
why: Without tail preservation, models can look better on average while silently becoming less useful to uncommon users and unusual cases — the populations least served by the bulk of the data.
key_works: Shumailov et al., 2023, *The Curse of Recursion*, arXiv:2305.17493; Gerstgrasser et al., 2024, *Is Model Collapse Inevitable?*, arXiv:2404.01413.

bib.title: Preserving rare tails during synthetic augmentation

title: Adaptive byte-level modeling without language penalties
open: Can a language model learn to segment raw byte streams at variable rates so that multilingual quality is preserved, corrupted or novel strings are handled gracefully, and computation follows the information content of the input rather than artifacts of a fixed tokenizer? Formally, the goal is adaptive segmentation and compute allocation driven by information content, not tokenization accidents.
status: The Byte Latent Transformer (Pagnani et al., 2024, *Byte Latent Transformer: Patches Scale Better Than Tokens*, arXiv:2412.09871) explored dynamic byte patching at scales up to 8 billion parameters in 2024, motivated in part by evidence that tokenizers introduce unfairness between languages (Petrov et al., 2023, arXiv:2305.15425); robustness, efficiency, and language equity have not yet been jointly demonstrated.
solved_when: A variable-rate byte-level segmentation method jointly demonstrates robustness, efficiency, and language equity — handling corrupted or novel strings, matching or improving multilingual quality, and allocating computation by information content — at scale.
why: It removes tokenizer brittleness and the uneven per-language costs that fixed vocabularies impose across writing systems, making byte-level modeling practical without penalizing any language.
key_works: Pagnoni et al., 2024, *Byte Latent Transformer: Patches Scale Better Than Tokens*, arXiv:2412.09871; Petrov et al., 2023, *Language Model Tokenizers Introduce Unfairness Between Languages*, arXiv:2305.15425.

bib.title: Adaptive byte-level modeling without language penalties

title: Optimal stopping for test-time reasoning
open: When should a reasoning model stop deliberating? We seek a principled stopping rule that halts test-time computation when the expected improvement in answer quality no longer justifies the added latency, expense, or risk — estimated online, without access to the correct answer or an oracle difficulty label.
status: Test-time compute allocation has demonstrated gains since 2024 (Snell et al., 2024, *Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally can be More Effective than Scaling Model Parameters*, arXiv:2408.03314), but a transferable stopping policy with reliable uncertainty remains a distinct target; related work in sequential analysis treats optimal stopping under misspecified observation models.
solved_when: A transferable stopping policy exists that decides, in real time during test-time reasoning, whether to continue or stop, with reliable uncertainty estimates, and that demonstrably avoids both premature stopping and unproductive deliberation across settings.
why: Without such a rule, systems either answer prematurely or burn compute on deliberation that yields nothing; a principled rule converts test-time compute from a fixed budget into a judiciously spent resource.
key_works: Snell et al., 2024, *Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally can be More Effective than Scaling Model Parameters*, arXiv:2408.03314.

bib.title: Optimal stopping for test-time reasoning

title: Position-invariant use of relevant context
open: Can a language model preserve answer quality when the same relevant evidence appears at different positions within a long context, with content and distractors held constant? The question extends beyond single-needle retrieval to whether multi-evidence reasoning can be position-invariant.
status: Position sensitivity was documented in 2023 by "Lost in the Middle" (Liu et al., 2023, *Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts*, arXiv:2307.03172; see also Bai et al., 2023, *LongBench*, arXiv:2308.14508). Longer advertised context windows do not by themselves establish position-invariant reasoning.
solved_when: A model demonstrates answer quality invariant to the placement of relevant evidence in long contexts — for both single-needle retrieval and multi-evidence reasoning — under evaluations holding content and distractors fixed.
why: A solution makes document order less likely to determine correctness, so long-context models would rely on relevance rather than position of evidence.
key_works: Liu et al., 2023, *Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts*, arXiv:2307.03172; Bai et al., 2023, *LongBench*, arXiv:2308.14508.

bib.title: Position-invariant use of relevant context

title: Revising memories without losing historical truth
open: Can a long-term memory system update its beliefs when facts change or earlier statements are corrected, while still preserving when each statement was believed and why — avoiding both stale answers and the rewriting of history?
status: LongMemEval (Wu et al., 2024, *LongMemEval: Benchmarking Chat Assistants on Long-Term Interactive Memory*, arXiv:2410.10813) includes knowledge-update and temporal-reasoning challenges; a robust memory model must distinguish correction, change, contradiction, and uncertainty.
solved_when: A memory model demonstrably distinguishes correction, change, contradiction, and uncertainty, and performs robustly on the knowledge-update and temporal-reasoning challenges of LongMemEval without losing the provenance or temporal record of past beliefs.
why: It enables dependable long-term assistance and auditability: a system whose remembered history can be trusted and inspected rather than silently overwritten.
key_works: Wu et al., 2024, *LongMemEval: Benchmarking Chat Assistants on Long-Term Interactive Memory*, arXiv:2410.10813.

bib.title: Revising memories without losing historical truth

title: Precise memory deletion without collateral forgetting
open: Can an AI system with both parametric and retrievable memory delete a specified fact or experience on request, leaving every other piece of knowledge untouched? Formally, deletion must be effective against paraphrases and inference-based probes, and the memory must remain safely updatable afterward, while unrelated knowledge and behavior are preserved.
status: Targeted editing methods such as ROME and MEMIT demonstrate that specific factual associations can be modified, and the TOFU benchmark evaluates unlearning of fine-tuned facts. However, editing an answer and eliminating recoverable information are not equivalent, and no method establishes verified deletion across paraphrase, inference, and later updates (Meng et al., 2022, arXiv:2202.05262; Maini et al., 2024, arXiv:2401.06121).
solved_when: A method exists that removes a targeted fact from both parametric and retrievable memory such that it cannot be recovered via paraphrased queries, inference, or subsequent updates, while performance on unrelated knowledge is demonstrably preserved.
why: It underpins practical user corrections, compliance with privacy deletion requests, and removal of poisoned or harmful memories — none of which are possible if deletion either fails or causes collateral forgetting.
key_works: Meng et al., 2022, *Locating and Editing Factual Associations in GPT*, arXiv:2202.05262; Maini et al., 2024, *TOFU*, arXiv:2401.06121.

bib.title: Precise memory deletion without collateral forgetting

title: Realistic longitudinal memory evaluation
open: Can we build a longitudinal memory evaluation for LLM assistants that mirrors real user histories — including forgotten details, changed preferences, contradictory reports, and multiple people — where all data is consented and answers cannot be recovered from superficial lexical cues? The goal is a benchmark whose answers require genuine long-horizon memory rather than surface matching, with errors carrying meaningful consequences for the score.
status: LoCoMo (Maharana et al., 2024, *Evaluating Very Long-Term Conversational Memory of LLM Agents*, arXiv:2402.17753) and LongMemEval (Wu et al., 2024, *LongMemEval*, arXiv:2410.10813) are concrete 2024 baselines; longer, more representative, and privacy-preserving evaluations remain an expansion target.
solved_when: A publicly available, consented, longitudinal benchmark exists that contains forgotten details, changed preferences, contradictory reports, and multiple people, meaningfully penalizes errors, and is verified to resist retrieval via superficial lexical cues; existing 2024 baselines (LoCoMo, LongMemEval) are surpassed in length, representativeness, and privacy preservation.
why: It separates genuine long-term assistance from benchmark-specific retrieval tricks, revealing which systems actually remember and reason over a user's history rather than exploit dataset artifacts.
key_works: Maharana et al., 2024, *Evaluating Very Long-Term Conversational Memory of LLM Agents*, arXiv:2402.17753; Wu et al., 2024, *LongMemEval*, arXiv:2410.10813.

bib.title: Realistic longitudinal memory evaluation

title: Out-of-distribution abstention with useful coverage
open: Can a language model recognize when it faces a situation unlike anything in its development data, and decline to answer at a controlled error rate — without refusing so often that it stops being useful? Formally, the goal is abstention with a useful coverage guarantee under distribution shifts not represented in the abstention system's development data.
status: Open-set recognition and LLM confidence estimation supply partial methods, but achieving useful coverage under genuinely novel shifts remains stronger than what thresholding on a familiar benchmark provides. Related statistics work on selective prediction under unknown distribution shift is pertinent (Bendale and Boult, 2015/2016, *Towards Open Set Deep Networks*, arXiv:1511.06233; Kadavath et al., 2022, *Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know*, arXiv:2207.05221).
solved_when: An abstention method demonstrably holds a controlled error rate on genuinely novel shifts while maintaining useful coverage, evaluated on shifts absent from the abstention system's development data — going beyond thresholding on a familiar benchmark.
why: It enables graceful failure when a model encounters conditions outside its competence, rather than confidently wrong answers; without it, deployed systems fail silently exactly where they are least reliable.
key_works: Bendale and Boult, 2015/2016, *Towards Open Set Deep Networks*, arXiv:1511.06233; Kadavath et al., 2022, *Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know*, arXiv:2207.05221.

bib.title: Out-of-distribution abstention with useful coverage

title: Predicting real deployment outcomes from benchmarks
open: Which benchmark measurements actually predict how a model performs once deployed — its error rates, productivity effects, user benefit, and harm? Formally, the task is to characterize and validate a mapping from benchmark results to real-world deployment outcomes, prospectively and across organizations and model updates.
status: Holistic evaluations such as HELM (Liang et al., 2022, *Holistic Evaluation of Language Models*, arXiv:2211.09110) broaden the dimensions measured, while realistic agent benchmarks like τ-bench (Yao et al., 2024, arXiv:2406.12045) move closer to actual workflows; however, external validity still requires field validation rather than assumed transfer.
solved_when: A validated, prospective mapping exists from benchmark measurements to deployed-outcome metrics (error rates, productivity, user benefit, harm), shown to hold across organizations and across model updates.
why: It stops organizations from optimizing benchmark scores that do not predict useful real-world outcomes, grounding evaluation in deployment reality.
key_works: Liang et al., 2022, *Holistic Evaluation of Language Models*, arXiv:2211.09110; Yao et al., 2024, *τ-bench*, arXiv:2406.12045.

bib.title: Predicting real deployment outcomes from benchmarks

title: Metamorphic tests for semantic invariance
open: Can we build a systematic library of transformations that perturb an input while either preserving the correct answer or changing it in a precisely predictable way, letting us detect when models violate these expectations? The library should span paraphrase, unit changes, entity renaming, document reordering, and irrelevant context.
status: Compositional and long-context benchmarks (e.g., Hsieh et al., 2023, *SugarCrepe*, arXiv:2306.14610; Liu et al., 2023, *Lost in the Middle*, arXiv:2307.03172) expose selected invariance failures, but a systematic transformation library with validated semantic preservation remains missing infrastructure.
solved_when: A systematic transformation library exists covering paraphrase, units, entity renaming, document order, and irrelevant context, with validated semantic preservation of its transformations, and it can be used to detect invariance violations in models.
why: Such tests expose brittle behavior without requiring a new gold answer for every example, making robustness evaluation cheap and scalable.
key_works: Hsieh et al., 2023, *SugarCrepe*, arXiv:2306.14610; Liu et al., 2023, *Lost in the Middle*, arXiv:2307.03172.

bib.title: Metamorphic tests for semantic invariance

title: Identifiability of learned interpretability features
open: Determine when different feature decompositions represent the same underlying computation and when they imply incompatible explanations. Supply uncertainty or equivalence classes rather than treating one dictionary as canonical.
status: Sparse-autoencoder research establishes useful decompositions and scaling methods. Nonuniqueness and dependence on training choices remain important residual questions.
why: Makes feature-level scientific claims reproducible.
key_works: Cunningham et al., 2023, *Sparse Autoencoders Find Highly Interpretable Features*, arXiv:2309.08600; Gao et al., 2024, *Scaling and evaluating sparse autoencoders*, arXiv:2406.04093.

bib.title: Identifiability of learned interpretability features

title: Faithful natural-language explanations
open: Can we generate natural-language explanations whose stated reasons are the factors that actually caused the model's answer, rather than post hoc rationalizations? Formally, can faithfulness be established through interventions — for example, perturbing the cited reason and checking that the answer changes accordingly?
status: 2023 studies demonstrated unfaithful chain-of-thought explanations and proposed tests for measuring faithfulness; fluent reasoning remains insufficient evidence of faithfulness (Turpin et al., 2023, *Language Models Don't Always Say What They Think*, arXiv:2305.04388; Lanham et al., 2023, *Measuring Faithfulness in Chain-of-Thought Reasoning*, arXiv:2307.13702).
solved_when: A method exists that produces explanations whose causal role is verified by intervention tests, such that fluent chain-of-thought is no longer accepted as sufficient evidence and unfaithful rationalizations can be reliably distinguished from faithful accounts.
why: Without faithfulness guarantees, explanations cannot support debugging or justified trust in model outputs, since a plausible-sounding rationale may have played no role in the answer.
key_works: Turpin et al., 2023, *Language Models Don’t Always Say What They Think*, arXiv:2305.04388; Lanham et al., 2023, *Measuring Faithfulness in Chain-of-Thought Reasoning*, arXiv:2307.13702.

title: Indirect prompt-injection resistance with preserved utility
open: Can we build an LLM agent that reads untrusted documents, webpages, messages, and tool outputs without letting that content change its authorized goals or permissions? The target is resistance to adaptive indirect prompt-injection attacks while still preserving the agent's ability to do useful work with those inputs.
status: Indirect injection was documented in 2023 by Greshake et al. (*Not what you've signed up for*, arXiv:2302.12173). AgentDojo and CaMeL provide evaluation and architectural defenses (Debenedetti et al., 2025, *Defeating Prompt Injections by Design*, arXiv:2503.18813). However, achieving utility-preserving coverage across heterogeneous applications remains a broader, open challenge.
solved_when: An agent design demonstrates robustness against adaptive indirect prompt-injection attacks while retaining useful document-processing utility, with that coverage holding across heterogeneous applications.
why: It protects agents that must consume adversarially supplied information — the common case for browsing, email, and tool-using assistants — without forcing a choice between security and usefulness.
key_works: Greshake et al., 2023, *Not what you’ve signed up for*, arXiv:2302.12173; Debenedetti et al., 2025, *Defeating Prompt Injections by Design*, arXiv:2503.18813.

bib.title: Indirect prompt-injection resistance with preserved utility

title: Valid membership-inference audits
open: Can we design a membership-inference audit that reliably detects whether specific texts were used in training, while controlling for confounders such as distribution mismatch, duplicated data, and public availability of the text? In formal terms, this is a hypothesis-testing problem where the audit must maintain tight control of its false-positive rate before any claim of training membership is made.
status: Membership inference has a foundational 2016–2017 literature (Shokri et al., 2016/2017, *Membership Inference Attacks against Machine Learning Models*, arXiv:1610.05820), and LLM data extraction (Carlini et al., 2020/2021, *Extracting Training Data from Large Language Models*, arXiv:2012.07805) provides a related but different privacy signal; related statistical work concerns hypothesis testing with extremely low tolerated false-positive rates. No audit meeting the stated controls and reporting standard yet exists.
solved_when: An experimental audit methodology exists that (i) measures training-membership leakage while controlling for distribution mismatch, duplicates, and public availability, and (ii) reports false-positive rates at levels suitable for consequential claims (i.e., extremely low tolerated false-positive rates).
why: A valid audit prevents both overlooked privacy leakage in deployed models and unsupported public accusations of training-data use, either of which carries real consequences for individuals and organizations.
key_works: Shokri et al., 2016/2017, *Membership Inference Attacks against Machine Learning Models*, arXiv:1610.05820; Carlini et al., 2020/2021, *Extracting Training Data from Large Language Models*, arXiv:2012.07805.

bib.title: Valid membership-inference audits

title: Certified unlearning for practically trained LLMs
open: When a deletion request arrives for a practically trained LLM, can we remove the influence of the specified training contributions with a certificate meaningfully related to retraining without those contributions — while preserving utility and without full retraining for every request?
status: Certified removal is known only for restricted model classes; the TOFU benchmark (Maini et al., 2024, arXiv:2401.06121) supplies an LLM unlearning benchmark, but behavioral suppression alone does not constitute a certified removal result. Foundations trace to Guo et al., 2019/2020, *Certified Data Removal from Machine Learning Models* (arXiv:1911.03030).
solved_when: A method exists that, for practically trained LLMs, produces a certificate tied to retraining-without-the-contributions, maintains utility on remaining tasks, and avoids full retraining per deletion request.
why: It makes deletion requests technically meaningful, turning a compliance obligation into a verifiable guarantee rather than behavioral suppression.
key_works: Guo et al., 2019/2020, *Certified Data Removal from Machine Learning Models*, arXiv:1911.03030; Maini et al., 2024, *TOFU*, arXiv:2401.06121.

bib.title: Certified unlearning for practically trained LLMs

title: Unlearning that survives later training
open: Can we make machine unlearning durable, so that information deleted from a model stays deleted even as the model continues its life through unrelated fine-tuning, merging with other models, retrieval from external memory, or encounters with correlated data? A satisfactory answer must also say when relearning from genuinely new authorized data should be considered permissible rather than a failure of unlearning.
status: Existing unlearning benchmarks and large-scale editing methods address immediate behavior after deletion (e.g., Maini et al., 2024, *TOFU*, arXiv:2401.06121; Meng et al., 2022/2023, *Mass-Editing Memory in a Transformer*, arXiv:2210.07229), but durability across a model's subsequent lifecycle is an additional requirement that current work does not establish. A related problem outside LLMs is durable revocation in replicated and derived data in information systems.
solved_when: A method exists for which removed information does not reappear after subsequent unrelated fine-tuning, model merging, memory retrieval, or exposure to correlated examples, with a defined criterion separating such reappearance from legitimate relearning from genuinely new authorized data, demonstrated experimentally.
why: Without durability, deletion is only a temporary surface effect: a model can silently resurrect supposedly removed information at any later stage of its lifecycle, defeating the purpose of unlearning for privacy and revocation.
key_works: Maini et al., 2024, *TOFU*, arXiv:2401.06121; Meng et al., 2022/2023, *Mass-Editing Memory in a Transformer*, arXiv:2210.07229.

bib.title: Unlearning that survives later training

title: Prompt revocation of delegated authority
subfield: Durable agent infrastructure and distributed execution
open: When a user withdraws authority from an agent, how far and how fast does that revocation actually travel — through running agents, queued actions, cached credentials, and delegated subagents? The goal is a revocation mechanism that propagates through all of these with explicit latency and failure guarantees.
status: Agent security architectures constrain execution, but revocation across persistent distributed work adds lifecycle requirements beyond initial authorization. Related work includes Debenedetti et al., 2025, *Defeating Prompt Injections by Design*, arXiv:2503.18813; and Gao et al., 2024, *AgentScope*, arXiv:2402.14034.
solved_when: Revocation demonstrably reaches running agents, queued actions, cached credentials, and delegated subagents, with the latency and failure guarantees stated explicitly and met.
why: Without propagation beyond initial authorization, users cannot genuinely withdraw access or stop the future effects of already-delegated work.
key_works: Debenedetti et al., 2025, *Defeating Prompt Injections by Design*, arXiv:2503.18813; Gao et al., 2024, *AgentScope*, arXiv:2402.14034.

bib.title: Prompt revocation of delegated authority

title: Diversity that actually reduces correlated agent errors
open: Can we construct ensembles of LLM agents whose disagreements reflect genuinely independent evidence or computation, rather than superficial persona variation, so that adding agents actually reduces correlated failures? Formally: build agent teams that, at matched total cost, measurably lower the rate of correlated errors compared to a baseline ensemble.
status: Multi-agent frameworks such as AutoGen (Wu et al., 2023, arXiv:2308.08155) enable building ensembles, but failure analyses (Cemri et al., 2025, *Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?*, arXiv:2503.13657) show that coordination and shared-error problems persist, and adding more agents need not provide independent verification.
solved_when: An ensemble construction is demonstrated whose correlated-failure rate is measurably reduced at matched total cost, with the reduction attributable to independent evidence or computation rather than persona variation.
why: It would make redundancy a real reliability mechanism for multi-agent systems, rather than an illusion of verification that fails exactly when a single agent would.
key_works: Wu et al., 2023, *AutoGen*, arXiv:2308.08155; Cemri et al., 2025, *Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?*, arXiv:2503.13657.

bib.title: Diversity that actually reduces correlated agent errors

title: Reliable visual attribute and relation binding
open: Can a vision-language model reliably attach the right attributes, actions, and relations to the right entities when a scene is crowded or compositionally novel, rather than falling back on language-only shortcuts? In other words, can it achieve robust compositional binding — the visual analogue of the classic binding problem — even when word order and co-occurrence statistics offer misleading cues?
status: Concrete compositional evaluations have existed since 2022–2023, notably Winoground (Thrush et al., 2022, arXiv:2204.03162) and SugarCrepe (Hsieh et al., 2023, arXiv:2306.14610). Existing evidence shows that strong aggregate vision-language scores do not imply robust binding. The problem remains open experimentally.
solved_when: A model demonstrates correct attribute and relation binding on compositional benchmarks such as Winoground and SugarCrepe in crowded and compositionally novel scenes, with performance that resists language-only shortcuts and cannot be explained by high aggregate vision-language scores alone.
why: It upgrades multimodal systems from bag-of-concepts recognition to precise visual reasoning about *which* entity has *which* property and stands in *which* relation — a prerequisite for trustworthy grounding in complex scenes.
key_works: Thrush et al., 2022, *Winoground*, arXiv:2204.03162; Hsieh et al., 2023, *SugarCrepe*, arXiv:2306.14610.

title: Transfer to genuinely new robot embodiments
open: Can a policy trained across many robots be transferred to a genuinely new robot — different kinematics, sensors, grippers, and action space — using only a small amount of new data? The challenge is to achieve transfer that is distinct from mere retraining on a closely related platform.
status: Open. Open X-Embodiment and Octo demonstrate cross-robot data aggregation and generalist policies (arXiv:2310.08864; arXiv:2405.12213), but broad, low-data transfer to unseen embodiments remains a stronger, unrealized goal.
solved_when: A generalist policy demonstrably transfers skills to an unseen embodiment with different kinematics, sensors, grippers, and action spaces using minimal new data, outperforming or avoiding full retraining on that platform.
why: It removes the need to rebuild the learning stack from scratch for every new robot, making generalist robot learning practical across heterogeneous fleets.
key_works: Open X-Embodiment Collaboration, 2023, *Open X-Embodiment*, arXiv:2310.08864; Octo Model Team, 2024, *Octo*, arXiv:2405.12213.

title: Off-policy evaluation with hidden confounding
subfield: Reinforcement learning, continual learning, and open-ended adaptation
open: Can we estimate a new policy's expected consequences from observational logs when the actions in those logs depended on unrecorded state? In formal terms, construct estimators that remain valid under hidden confounding, yielding honest uncertainty quantification or partial-identification bounds whenever point identification fails.
status: Offline RL formalizes the evaluation of new policies from logged experience, but real operational data can violate the assumptions needed for ordinary estimators, leaving evaluation under hidden confounding unresolved.
solved_when: A method exists that, given confounded observational logs, returns either valid confidence statements or partial-identification bounds for the value of a candidate policy, with correctness guarantees that do not require the unconfoundedness assumptions of ordinary estimators.
why: It prevents unsafe policy deployment decisions based on biased retrospective estimates drawn from real operational data.
key_works: Levine et al., 2020, *Offline Reinforcement Learning*, arXiv:2005.01643; Chaney et al., 2017/2018, *How Algorithmic Confounding in Recommendation Systems Increases Homogeneity and Decreases Utility*, arXiv:1710.11214.

title: Measuring AI incidents without denominator blindness
open: Can we measure the real-world risk of AI systems by estimating incident rates and severity rather than by counting reported incidents? The task is to build statistically meaningful estimates that combine exposure denominators, consistent classification of what counts as an incident, and correction for reporting bias, so that raw report counts are never mistaken for population risk.
status: The AI Incident Database (McGregor, 2020/2021, *Preventing Repeated Real World AI Failures by Cataloging Incidents: The AI Incident Database*, arXiv:2011.08512) established an important cataloging approach in 2020–2021, but catalogs alone do not identify incidence rates; the problem is analogous to epidemiological surveillance with underreporting and uncertain exposure.
solved_when: There exists a methodology (and supporting data) that produces incident rate and severity estimates for AI deployments with explicit exposure denominators, consistent incident classifications, and reporting-bias correction, validated well enough that trends over time or across systems can be compared rather than merely catalogued.
why: Without denominators and bias correction, we cannot tell whether AI is getting safer or whether reporting is just getting better, which makes safety trends and the effectiveness of interventions unmeasurable.
key_works: McGregor, 2020/2021, *Preventing Repeated Real World AI Failures by Cataloging Incidents: The AI Incident Database*, arXiv:2011.08512.

title: Discriminating tests for AI consciousness and welfare relevance
open: Can we build empirical tests that actually discriminate between competing theories of consciousness as applied to artificial systems — separating mere verbal self-report from functional indicators, and explicitly representing moral uncertainty about the outcome?
status: Butlin et al. (2023, *Consciousness in Artificial Intelligence: Insights from the Science of Consciousness*, arXiv:2308.08708) synthesized theory-derived indicator properties from the scientific study of consciousness. Their work carries no implication that present systems are conscious, and no settled discriminating test yet resolves the question.
solved_when: A validated experimental methodology exists that yields theory-specific, empirically distinguishable verdicts about consciousness indicators in artificial systems, with verbal self-report, functional indicators, and moral uncertainty treated as separate, measurable components.
why: Such tests would let developers and regulators make cautious, evidence-based decisions about the welfare relevance of future AI systems rather than relying on untestable intuition.
key_works: Butlin et al., 2023, *Consciousness in Artificial Intelligence: Insights from the Science of Consciousness*, arXiv:2308.08708.
